Do not pair ragg with showtext-only fonts. dev: "ragg_png" --- ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: ## Inspiration Look at this fabric map of Africa:
![Africa Fabric Map: What's your next T-Shirt?](../../../../../materials/images/Africa-Fabric-Map.jpeg){#fig-africa-textile}
And look at this map of Nobel prize winners! ![Network of Nobel Prize Winners](../../../../../materials/images/NobelPrizeNetwork.png){#fig-nobel-winners} Would there be anything in common between these two 😮 ??!! How???!!! ## Introduction The South Indian tradition of Kolam, and the [Angolan tradition of Lusona](https://www.sahistory.org.za/sites/default/files/archive-files3/paulus_gerdes_lunda_geometry_mirror_curves_desbook4you.pdf) art have quite a few things in common. Both are also strongly linked to finite grammars and networks. ## {{< iconify icons8 idea >}} Inspiration

Click to generate a fresh Kolam!
## Creating Kolams How do we create these Kolam Patterns? Let us do this two ways: first pretending we are a South-Indian Woman adorning her doorstep in the morning. And then with two other methods, that lend themselves to computation / iteration. So, first by hand! ### Method #1: By Hand! See if you can manually mimic some of the moves here! As an exercise, try to ***anchor your elbow and forearm to the table***, and draw the pattern by rotating the paper! What are your observations? ::: {layout-ncol=3} ![](../../../../../materials/gifs/3-3a.gif) ![](../../../../../materials/gifs/3-3b.gif) ![](../../../../../materials/gifs/3-3c.gif) ::: ::: {layout-ncol=3} ![](../../../../../materials/gifs/3-3d.gif) ![](../../../../../materials/gifs/3-3e.gif) ![](../../../../../materials/gifs/3-3f.gif) ::: ::: {layout-ncol=3} ![](../../../../../materials/gifs/3-3g.gif) ![](../../../../../materials/gifs/3-3h.gif) ![](../../../../../materials/gifs/3-3i.gif) ::: ### Method #2: Using **Canonical Pieces** What does **canonical piece** mean? These are pieces like the alphabet: pieces that can be repeatedly used to create a vast variety of patterns? Sounds familiar again? Check the Polypad: :::{}
::: Here we use "pieces of Kolam" that are standard: by repeated usage of combinations of these pieces, ( I believe ) any kolam can be produced. Here is a video showing kolams with a few **canonical pieces**: :::{}
{{< video https://youtu.be/-l9za7UlzKM width=500 height=360 >}} Using "Canonical Pieces" by Saty Raghavachary
::: Which are the canonical pieces here? This is also the idea embedded in this toy called [Kolam Tiles](https://kolamtiles.com/). See this [YT Playlist on Kolam Tiles](https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PL6LYOn0Nvs_spbp4kYo2llyTmwPbFdEUf&si=ThsBwebTaEYInKNr). This program called Forkphorus gives a point-and-click interface to place canonical kolam tiles to achieve a design. ::: {.content-hidden} ::: {layout-ncol=2} ![](../../../../../materials/gifs/kolam3_howto.gif) ![](../../../../../materials/gifs/kolam4_howto.gif) ::: ::: {layout-ncol=2} ![](../../../../../materials/gifs/kolam6_howto.gif) ![](../../../../../materials/gifs/kolam7_howto.gif) ::: ::: {layout-ncol=2} ![](../../../../../materials/gifs/kolam9_howto.gif) ![](../../../../../materials/gifs/kolam10_howto.gif) ::: ::: This very accessible paper by Nagata and Thamburaj illustrates this concept and may help in recreating this idea digitally, in `p5.js`! {{< pdf ../../../../../materials/pdfs/Kolam/Nagata-Thamburaj-DigitalizationKolamPatterns.pdf >}} ### Method #2: Using Mirrors and Light This follows the development of [Paul Gerdes](https://www.mi.sanu.ac.rs/vismath/paulus/index.html). {{< html https://www.mi.sanu.ac.rs/vismath/paulus/pg1.htm height="500px" width="500px" >}} First let us get a printable grid to make our Kolams manually, since making grids can become tedious when you are making a lot of Kolams. We can use the grid to place "pulli-s" on the grid to make our Kolam. Head off to: and open it in your p5.js web-editor. Print out a few samples of the `.svg` grid file that is generated. Now consider that each of your Kolam "lines" or "trajectories" is [made of light](https://www.imaginary.org/program/frozenlight). And place some single horizontal or vertical mirrors, at some locations *midway between adjacent pulli-s*. See the figure below: ![Kolam with Mirrors](../../../../../materials/gifs/Kolam-With-Mirrors.png){#fig-kolam-with-mirrors} The black lines here are to be imagined as *"made of light"*. Whenever they hit a mirror, a *"curved reflection"* occurs. Note how the arrangement of mirrors is symmetric here. Can we take *computational liberties* here and make asymmetric mirror arrangements? Can the grid also be non-square? Try? ## The Mathematics of Kolam We will follow the *Lunda Geometry* treatment of Gerdes here, and also briefly( Ha! Briefly!!) touch upon the S. Jablan's treatment based on *Knot Theory*. TBWU. - Combine Karnaugh Maps, Network Adjacency Matrics, Cayley Symmetry Matrices, and Paulus Gerdus' Modulo-m Lunda matrices into a unified "Kolam Symmetry Matrix". - Discuss the similarity to Wang tiles. Questions: - Can we generate random KSMs and find "symmetry on average", in the manner of Field and Golubitsky? - Can we mimic Kolam Tiles / Saty Raghavachary's video in code? - How "simple" can the code be? ### Basics of Lunda Geometry and Kolam For more inspiration, see [here](https://www.mi.sanu.ac.rs/vismath/paulus/pg1.htm). This is a multipage article with many different grid+mirror arrangements! There is also an intriguing technique shown therein of **colouring the squares in the grid** alternatively white and black, to generate very symmetric shaded patterns! ### Kolams and Knot Theory S. Jablan's treatment based on *Knot Theory* ## Kolams with Code Work in (slow....) Progress!!! ::: {.panel-tabset .nav-pills style="background: whitesmoke;"} ### Using p5.js ```{=html}
``` ### Using R ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ggplot2) library(dplyr) # ========== STEP 1: Canonical pieces ========== # Each piece is a list of line segments inside the unit square [0,1]×[0,1] # Ports: which sides it connects (N=1, E=2, S=3, W=4) pieces <- list( straight_h = list(segs = data.frame(x = c(0, 1), y = c(0.5, 0.5)), ports = c(2, 4)), straight_v = list(segs = data.frame(x = c(0.5, 0.5), y = c(0, 1)), ports = c(1, 3)), turn_ne = list(segs = data.frame(x = c(0.5, 1), y = c(1, 0.5)), ports = c(1, 2)), turn_nw = list(segs = data.frame(x = c(0, 0.5), y = c(0.5, 1)), ports = c(1, 4)), turn_se = list(segs = data.frame(x = c(0.5, 1), y = c(0, 0.5)), ports = c(2, 3)), turn_sw = list(segs = data.frame(x = c(0, 0.5), y = c(0.5, 0)), ports = c(3, 4)), bounce_h = list(segs = data.frame(x = c(0, 0.5, 1), y = c(0.5, 0.3, 0.5)), ports = c(2, 4)), # mirror-like bounce_v = list(segs = data.frame(x = c(0.5, 0.3, 0.5), y = c(0, 0.5, 1)), ports = c(1, 3)) ) piece_names <- names(pieces) # ========== STEP 2: Sampling & aligning ========== m <- 6 n <- 8 set.seed(123) # sample a piece for every cell grid <- expand.grid(i = 1:n, j = 1:m) %>% mutate(piece = sample(piece_names, n(), replace = TRUE)) # expand into drawable segments, translated to cell position draw_data <- grid %>% rowwise() %>% do({ p <- pieces[[.$piece]] data.frame( i = .$i, j = .$j, x = p$segs$x + .$i - 1, y = p$segs$y + .$j - 1, group = paste(.$i, .$j, sep = "_") ) }) %>% ungroup() # optional: dots at cell centres (classic sona reference points) dots <- expand.grid(x = 0.5:(n - 0.5), y = 0.5:(m - 0.5)) # plot ggplot() + geom_point(data = dots, aes(x, y), colour = "grey50", size = 2) + geom_path( data = draw_data, aes(x, y, group = group), colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 1.2 ) + coord_fixed() + theme_void() + labs(title = "Randomly sampled canonical pieces → sona/Kolam attempt") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-1-1.png){fig-align='center' width=75%} ::: ::: ::: ## {{< iconify mingcute thought-line >}} Wait, But Why? Kolams and Sona are powerful metaphors for [graphs and networks](../../../../Analytics/Descriptive/Modules/100-Networks/index.qmd). These ideas show up in a variety of situations, such as tranportation networks, supply-chain, friendship networks, tracing literary and artistic influence, and so on. ## {{< iconify ooui references-ltr >}} References 1.
